office.title: Indiana School Board Member
office.summary: A school board is the elected or appointed governing body of a public school corporation, the legal unit that runs a local school district [1, 2]. The board hires and evaluates the superintendent, adopts policies, and approves the annual budget, while the superintendent and staff run schools day to day [3]. Most boards have five or seven members serving staggered four-year terms [3]. Starting in 2026, candidates may list a political party, run as independents, or list no affiliation on the ballot, and there is no primary for these seats [2, 4].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years, with elections staggered so part of the board is chosen every two years [3]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: At the November general election (November 3, 2026, or November 2028 for some seats); depending on the local organization plan, members represent the whole school corporation (at large) or a district within it, and some boards are wholly or partly appointed [2]

facts.label: Ballot label
facts.value: Each candidate chooses a party label, 'Independent', or no affiliation, shown next to the name; no primary and no straight-ticket voting for these races [2, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: Set by board resolution: an annual amount of no more than 10% of the lowest starting teacher salary in the school corporation, plus a capped per diem [5]

duties: Hires, evaluates and can dismiss the superintendent, and approves the hiring and firing of principals, teachers and other staff recommended by the superintendent [1, 7, 3].
Adopts the annual budget, appropriates funds and oversees school finances [1, 3].

Decides whether to ask voters to approve an operating referendum (an extra property tax levy); the board adopts the resolution and the Department of Local Government Finance reviews the ballot language for compliance with state law [8].
Approves contracts, buys and sells property, and decides on construction, repair and demolition of school buildings [1].

Bargains with the teachers' union over salary, wages and wage-related benefits such as health insurance and retirement; state law excludes teacher evaluation procedures from those bargaining subjects [9].
Writes and updates policies and rules for schools, often in a policy handbook, including the student handbook [1, 3].
Buys curricular materials, provides them to students without charge, and runs programs such as student transportation and school lunch [1].

Must adopt a process for parents and residents to ask that library material be removed as obscene or harmful to minors, review requests at public meetings and keep a public catalog of library materials [10].
Hears written appeals of student expulsions, unless the board has voted not to hear them [11].
Must take official action openly; Indiana's Open Door Law says public agencies' official action is to be conducted openly so the people may be fully informed [12, 13].

A school board member must have lived in the school corporation (and, for a district seat, the district) for at least one year before the election, and a teacher or other employee of the school corporation may not serve on its board [2].

What the board does not control: the State Board of Education adopts statewide academic standards [14], the General Assembly sets the state school funding formula in the state budget [15], and voucher (Choice Scholarship) eligibility is set by state law [16].
recent_changes: 2025: Senate Enrolled Act 287 allowed school board candidates to declare a party affiliation; the Indiana School Boards Association opposed the change, and a supporter quoted by WNDU, a Noblesville school board member, said it adds transparency [17].

2026: Candidates choose a party, 'Independent' or no affiliation on their nominating petition, and that choice appears on the ballot; a candidate claiming the Democratic or Republican party must have voted in that party's primary in the two most recent primaries they voted in, or have certification from the county party chair, or can be challenged and removed from the ballot [2].

July 2026: Chalkbeat reported, citing Indiana School Boards Association data, that 524 of 1,044 candidates chose a party, about 72% of them Republicans [18]; the Indiana Election Division's 2026 guidance and the wording of the law differ on the primary-voting test, a question county election boards decide [19].

February 2026: Senate Enrolled Act 25 set the order of school board candidates on the ballot, grouped by party, with candidates who list no affiliation placed after the party and independent candidates [20].

2025: Senate Enrolled Act 1, a property tax law, limits how much operating revenue districts can raise through taxes and restricts school referendums to statewide general elections in even-numbered years [21, 22].
2025: The same law requires districts to share operating revenue with brick-and-mortar charter schools that enroll their students, statewide starting in 2028 [21, 22].
2025: The state budget opened Choice Scholarship vouchers to all Indiana families starting in June 2026 [16].
2026: The Indianapolis Public Education Corporation, rather than the Indianapolis Public Schools board, now certifies Indianapolis Public Schools referendum questions for the ballot [20].

2023: Senate Enrolled Act 391 changed the so-called $1 law so the Indiana Department of Education can order districts that lost at least 10% of enrollment over five years to close schools under 60% capacity and offer them to charter schools [23].
2023: House Enrolled Act 1447 required school districts to set up procedures for complaints that library material is obscene or harmful to minors [10].

race_context: Brownsburg Community School Corporation (BCSC) serves Brown and Lincoln townships in Hendricks County [24, 25]. It reported 10,654 students in pre-K through grade 12 at the midpoint of the 2025-26 school year and 631 certified teachers; Kat Jessup is superintendent [26].

The five-member board serves four-year terms [27]. Seats: three Lincoln Township (Katie Dixon, president, term ending December 2026; Mike Wells; Matthew Freije), one Brown Township (Gordon Hayward, secretary) and one at-large (Jessica Heffernan, vice president, term ending December 2026) [24].

Two seats are on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot, one each, matching the state list's "vote for 1" [24, 6]. At-large: Heffernan is not on the ballot, so the seat is open; three candidates are running [24, 27]. Lincoln Township: incumbent Dixon faces Garen Carnes [24, 27]. Aurora Verkamp is listed with the American Solidarity Party; the other four are listed as nonpartisan [6].

Budget: BCSC says the 2023 law HB 1454 removed about $3.5 million a year from its Operations Fund and that SEA 1 (2025) removes more than $2 million a year more, requiring $7.9 million in cuts over three school years [25]. The district says it will start 2026-27 with 49 fewer staff and teacher positions, cutting $3.3 million, with more cuts expected in 2027-28 [25].

Referendum: BCSC has no operating referendum and said it will not seek one in 2026, calling a referendum "an absolute last resort" [25]. It says it collects and spends less per student than similar districts while outperforming them on state metrics [25].

Local support: the Town of Brownsburg approved a one-time $800,000 in TIF funds for BCSC workforce-development programs, and the Brown and Lincoln township trustees each pledged $100,000 toward transportation for homeless students under the McKinney-Vento program, which the district says costs over $300,000 a year [25].
Community engagement: the district held three public finance sessions (Feb. 4, Feb. 25 and March 18, 2026) on school funding, SEA 1 and possible 2027-28 cuts [25].
Forums: no candidate forum or news coverage of the 2026 race was found in reviewed sources. Ballotpedia surveys from Verkamp and Barker were the only detailed candidate statements found [28, 29].

candidates.summary: Homeschooling parent and Hendricks County native running for the open at-large seat; listed with the American Solidarity Party [28, 6].
background: Stay-at-home parent; graduated from the Indiana Academy for Science, Mathematics and Humanities and Indiana State University [28].
A Hendricks County native who attended Pittsboro Elementary and Tri-West [28].
Homeschools her children, who do not attend BCSC; she says a strong school system is a priority for every Brownsburg resident [28].
path_to_ballot: Listed with the American Solidarity Party on the 2026 ballot list [6].

items: Says teachers need flexibility to adapt lesson plans to the children in front of them rather than follow a rigid schedule, even one developed by district teachers [28].
Says "Having the best test scores should not be the goal" and that schools should teach children how to learn [28].
Wants significant outdoor time and physical movement, especially for elementary-age children [28].
Says charter and magnet schools offer flexibility BCSC should use to enhance its offerings, while acknowledging this would require significant resources and time [28].

on_incumbent: No comment on the current board's decisions was found.
plans: Says she looks forward to learning about BCSC from community members and through the Vision BCSC program [28].
endorsements_finance: No endorsements or campaign finance reports were found in reviewed sources.
gaps: No news coverage of her candidacy was found.
No stated position on the budget cuts or SEA 1 was found.
Campaign finance filings with Hendricks County were not reviewed.

candidates.summary: Candidate for the open at-large seat, listed as nonpartisan; little public information was found [6, 30].
background: No background information was found in reviewed sources [30].
path_to_ballot: Listed as nonpartisan on the 2026 ballot list [6].
endorsements_finance: No endorsements or campaign finance reports were found in reviewed sources.
gaps: Did not complete Ballotpedia's survey; his campaign Facebook page could not be read; no news coverage was found.

candidates.summary: Healthcare executive and BCSC parent running for the open at-large seat, listed as nonpartisan [29, 6].
background: Has more than 20 years of leadership experience in healthcare organizations in strategy, operations and finance; bachelor's degree from Erskine College [29].
Brownsburg resident since 2014 and parent of two BCSC students; in her fourth year on her elementary school's PSG board, now as president; graduate of the district's Vision BCSC program [29].
path_to_ballot: Listed as nonpartisan on the 2026 ballot list [6].

items: Says fiscal responsibility means understanding alternatives, seeking efficiencies, advocating for a sustainable funding structure and avoiding savings that create larger costs later [29].
Says programs should be evaluated on outcomes, need, participation and cost, and the district should be willing to ask "what we can stop doing" [29].
Says core classroom instruction should come first when resources are limited [29].
Calls teacher retention critical, citing pay, workload, leadership, resources and professional growth [29].
Wants a consistent process for major decisions: explain the issue and trade-offs early, take community input before deciding, then explain what was decided and why [29].

on_incumbent: Says she wants "greater transparency and community understanding around significant decisions and changes," noting that current decisions are financial; no direct criticism of specific board votes was found [29].
plans: Says she would help protect what makes Brownsburg schools strong while navigating financial challenges [29].
endorsements_finance: No endorsements or campaign finance reports were found in reviewed sources.
gaps: No news coverage of her candidacy was found; her employer was not named.
Campaign finance filings with Hendricks County were not reviewed.

candidates.summary: Incumbent Lincoln Township member and board president, first elected in 2022; listed as nonpartisan [24, 27, 6].
background: Listed by the district as Dr. Katie Dixon, board president, representing Lincoln Township [24].
path_to_ballot: Listed as nonpartisan on the 2026 ballot list [6].
Ran for the Lincoln Township seat in 2022 against Tiffany Dearman and Joseph Mgboh; her current term expires December 2026 [27, 24].
